questions.learningObjective: Convert trigonometric form into rectangular form
questions.stem: Explain how to convert a complex number written in trigonometric form into rectangular form.

answer.exemplar: A number in trigonometric form is r times the sum of cos of an angle and i times the sine of that angle. Multiplying out gives a real part of r cos theta and an imaginary part of r sin theta. For instance 3 times the sum of cos 60 degrees and i sin 60 degrees becomes 1.5 plus 2.6i, so the modulus fixes the distance from the origin and the angle fixes the direction.

questions.explanation: Trigonometric form packs the modulus and the angle into one expression. Expanding the sine and cosine terms separates the real and imaginary coordinates of the point.
questions.hint: Multiply the modulus by the cosine and by the sine.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish polar form from the argument
questions.stem: Explain the difference between the polar form of a complex number and its argument.

answer.exemplar: Polar form writes a complex number as a modulus r times the sum of cos theta and i sin theta, packing the size and direction of the number into one expression. The argument theta alone is the angle the number makes with the positive real axis. Because angles differing by a full turn describe the same direction, the argument is only defined modulo 360 degrees unless a specific branch is chosen.

questions.explanation: The modulus is the distance from the origin and the argument is the direction. Polar form combines them multiplicatively, while the argument on its own is only meaningful modulo a full turn.
questions.hint: One is the size, the other is the direction.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how multiplication affects moduli and arguments
questions.stem: Explain how multiplying two complex numbers affects their moduli and their arguments.

answer.exemplar: If z equals r times the sum of cos alpha and i sin alpha and w equals s times the sum of cos beta and i sin beta, then the product zw equals rs times the sum of cos of alpha plus beta and i sin of alpha plus beta. questions.explanation: Multiplication of complex numbers multiplies their lengths and adds their directions. This is the reason polar form is so convenient for repeated multiplication.
questions.hint: Moduli multiply and arguments add.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to choose between the two triangle laws
questions.stem: Explain how to decide between the law of sines and the law of cosines for a given set of measurements.

answer.exemplar: The law of sines needs one side together with its opposite angle, and it then finds the other angles or sides, though it may leave two possible triangles. The law of cosines needs two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides, and it finds the remaining side or angle uniquely. If an angle opposite a known side is given, the sine law is the natural choice.

questions.explanation: The sine law works from a side and its opposite angle, and it can produce two candidates. The cosine law works from two sides with the included angle, or from three sides, and always gives a single result.
questions.hint: Ask which quantities you actually know.

answer.exemplar: The area of a triangle with two sides a and b enclosing the angle C can be built by placing the triangle in a rectangle whose sides are a and b. options.text: Replace the leading 2 with 4, since both coordinates must double
options.misconception: believes the modulus must be applied twice to each coordinate

options.text: Flip both signs, so the real part is -1 and the imaginary part is positive
Swap the coordinates, so the imaginary part is -1 and the real part is root of 3

options.misconception: believes a third-quadrant angle produces positive coordinates

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to obtain polar form from rectangular form
questions.stem: Explain how to obtain the polar form of a complex number that is written in rectangular form.

answer.exemplar: Given x plus yi, the modulus is the square root of x squared plus y squared and the argument is the angle of the point, found with the inverse tangent of y over x after choosing the correct quadrant. For 3 plus 4i the modulus is 5 and the argument is about 53.13 degrees, so the polar form is 5 times the sum of cos 53.13 degrees and i sin 53.13 degrees.

questions.explanation: The modulus comes from the distance formula applied to the coordinates. The argument needs both the reference angle and the quadrant of the point, since the inverse tangent alone loses that information.
questions.hint: Distance gives the modulus, the quadrant gives the angle.

options.misconception: adds 180 degrees but does not reduce the angle into the principal range

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the modulus is never negative
questions.stem: Explain why the modulus of a complex number is always non-negative.

answer.exemplar: The modulus is defined as the square root of x squared plus y squared for the number x plus yi, so it is built from a square root of a sum of squares and can never be negative. Because it represents the length of the segment from the origin to the point, a length of zero would mean the point sits at the origin itself.

questions.explanation: The modulus is a distance computed by a square root, so it is automatically non-negative. It equals zero only for the number at the origin.
questions.hint: A square root of a sum of squares cannot be negative.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the ambiguous case influences law choice
questions.stem: Explain how the ambiguous case influences the choice of law for reef survey data.

answer.exemplar: The law of sines can produce two possible triangles when a side and its opposite angle are known and the other side is longer, because the computed sine value matches both an angle and its supplement. The law of cosines avoids this because two sides and the included angle determine a single triangle. Surveyors therefore reach for the cosine law whenever they have two sides and the angle between them.

questions.explanation: Knowing which inputs you have tells you which law applies and whether ambiguity can arise. Two sides with the included angle remove the ambiguity completely, while a side with its opposite angle may not.
questions.hint: The pattern of the known data decides the law.

questions.topic: Triangle area from two sides and an angle
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to find an area from two sides and an angle
questions.stem: Explain how to find the area of a triangle when only two sides and the angle between them are known.

answer.exemplar: The area of a triangle with sides a and b enclosing angle C is one half ab sin C, which follows by taking b sin C as the perpendicular height above the base a. With a equal to 4, b equal to 6 and C equal to 30 degrees the area is one half of 24 times one half, which is 6 square units. No third side is needed at all.

questions.explanation: The perpendicular height of the triangle is one side times the sine of the included angle, so the area follows directly from the two sides and that angle. Finding the third side first would be extra work.
questions.hint: The height is one side times the sine of the included angle.
